$comment:
**Classified `safe`, and the range is what buys it.** The easy reading is that recolouring a flash the game already draws is aesthetic and therefore fits §6.1's second allowlist category without an argument. For hue that is true. For `intensity` it very nearly was not, and the fix was to define the number rather than to defend it: `intensity` is a fraction of **vanilla's own hurt-overlay alpha**, not an absolute strength, so 1 is exactly what Minecraft already draws and there is no value above it. The mod cannot make a landed hit more visible than the game made it; it can only make it a different colour, or less visible. That is the same move `fov` made — "the range is exactly vanilla's own slider" — and it is deliberate here, because the alternative was shipping a slider whose top end made a hit readable that vanilla left ambiguous and then arguing about whether that counted. A number that cannot cross the line does not need the argument.

Two things are **not** what carries the classification, and they are named so that a later change to either does not silently move the mod. `own_hits_only` is a legibility default, not a safety gate: the tint vanilla draws on an entity somebody *else* hit is already on your screen, at the same alpha, for the same hurt ticks, so recolouring it reveals nothing — it only makes a worse cue. And this mod does not touch the first-person damage overlay, the red flash on your own screen when you are hit. `overlay`'s `settings_description` records that switch being cut from that mod for removing a combat cue rather than an occluder, and it stays cut; this is `RenderLivingBase`'s entity tint and nothing else.

**`color` owns hue, `intensity` owns alpha, and they must not both own alpha.** `#/definitions/hex_color` accepts `#RRGGBBAA` and `crosshair.color` ships the eight-digit form, so nothing in the schema stops a player storing an alpha byte here. The actuator drops it: `intensity` is the single owner. Two owners of one alpha is `toggle_sneak`'s "two owners of one latch" with a different noun, and the failure it produces is a player dragging `intensity` to its top and seeing nothing because their colour ends in `00` — silent, and blamed on the wrong setting. The default is six digits for that reason. Narrowing the `$ref` in place is not possible in draft-07 (a `$ref` sibling is ignored), so this note and the description below are the enforcement until the newtype in `crates/void-loadout/src/mods.rs` grows one.

What would move this to `grey`: `intensity` gaining any range above vanilla's alpha; a duration or persistence setting of any kind, because a tint that outlives vanilla's `hurtTime` is a hit *marker* rather than a recolour, and a marker is a different mod and a `grey` one; or tinting an entity vanilla did not tint.
label: Hit colour
description: Recolours the red flash the game draws on an entity you hit.
settings_description:
Settings for the Hit colour gameplay mod. §3.2 #5's verdict is "Entity-render tint; genuinely helps read whether a hit landed", and the reason it helps is not that the flash is missing — it is that vanilla drew it in the one colour a 1.8 PvP screen is already full of. The mod is a hue swap in the entity hurt overlay and an alpha the player can lower; it changes nothing about when the flash fires, how long it lasts, or which entities get one, and the `$comment` at the top of this file is the whole §11 briefing for why those three are the constraints rather than the settings.

It is `kind: gameplay` although it draws, for `hitboxes`' reason: `kind` splits on whether the mod owns a draggable HUD item, and a tint on somebody else's model has nowhere to be placed. `_shared.json`'s gameplay block says so directly.
source: the entity hurt overlay applied in RenderLivingBase#setBrightness

color.description: Colour the hurt overlay is drawn in. `#2FB8A6` by default, and deliberately not vanilla's red, for two reasons that are both about the rest of the screen. A mod that turns on and changes nothing looks broken — that is the argument that withdrew `old_animations` from the last wave — and a default of `#FF0000` would be exactly that mod. More to the point, red is the worst available choice on a 1.8 map: it is the nether, it is lava, it is red wool and red leather in Bedwars, and as of this same wave it is the low-health vignette `damage_tint` draws at the edge of the same frame. The two most decision-shaped cues on screen should not be the same hue. Teal is far from all of them and is a colour the product already owns (`--teal` in `packages/ui/src/tokens.css`), so the default is a choice somebody already defended rather than a new hex. Six digits and not eight: the alpha byte belongs to `intensity`, and if one is written here it is dropped — see the top of this file. Expect players who live in one mode to retune this, which is why it is a colour and not a switch.
color.$comment: `$ref: hex_color_rgb`, the six-digit definition, rather than the shared `hex_color`. `intensity` is the sole owner of alpha on this mod — it is a fraction of vanilla's own hurt-overlay strength, which is what keeps the mod `safe` rather than `grey` — so a byte stored here would be a second owner of one value. Every consumer already dropped it; this is the contract agreeing with them rather than relying on them, and it gives Rust a validating newtype that rejects it on load.

own_hits_only.description: Whether the recolour applies only to entities you damaged, or to every entity the game tints. On by default, because the mod is hit *confirmation* and a confirmation that also fires when two other players hit each other across the arena is not one — you would be reading somebody else's fight in your own colour, in your peripheral vision, during yours. Off is for spectating and for the team modes where knowing a teammate connected is worth the noise. It is not what makes this mod `safe`, and the top of this file says why in as many words: a setting everybody believes is load-bearing is a setting nobody dares change.

intensity.description: Alpha of the recoloured overlay, as a fraction of the alpha vanilla already draws it at — 1 is the game's own, 0 draws nothing. **Not an absolute strength**, and that distinction is the entire §11 argument at the top of this file: there is no value here that makes a landed hit more visible than Minecraft made it, which is what keeps a recolour inside "purely aesthetic". 1 by default, because a player enabling this wants the flash they already had, in a colour they can pick out. Lower values are for the player who finds a full-strength tint on a model they are standing next to more distracting than useful; 0 is the honest way to say "recolour nothing", and it costs you the cue rather than buying you anything — which is the direction §6.1 has never had an objection to.
